A dermatologist is a medical doctor who specializes in diagnosing and treating conditions related to the skin, hair, and nails.

Think of your body as having different systems — your heart, lungs, bones, and so on. Each system has a specialist doctor. A dermatologist is the specialist for the outer layer of your body: your skin (the largest organ you have), your hair, and your nails.

A dermatologist's work falls into a few broad areas:

1. Medical work — treating diseases and disorders
This is the bulk of their work. They diagnose and treat conditions like:

  • Acne (pimples and breakouts)
  • Eczema (dry, itchy, inflamed skin)
  • Psoriasis (scaly, red patches on skin)
  • Fungal infections (like ringworm or athlete's foot)
  • Skin allergies and rashes
  • Hair loss (such as alopecia)
  • Nail infections or abnormalities
  • Skin cancer — one of the most critical parts of their job

2. Surgical work — procedures on the skin
Dermatologists are also trained to perform minor and sometimes major procedures. For example:

  • Removing moles, cysts, or warts
  • Biopsies (cutting a small piece of skin to test it in a lab)
  • Treating skin cancer by surgically removing it
  • Draining skin abscesses (pockets of infection)

3. Cosmetic work — improving appearance
Some dermatologists also help people with appearance-related concerns, not just medical ones. This includes:

  • Treating wrinkles
  • Reducing scars or dark spots
  • Laser treatments for unwanted hair or pigmentation
  • Botox and fillers (though some people debate whether this is strictly "medical")
How a Dermatologist Is Different From a Regular Doctor

A general doctor (called a primary care physician or family doctor) knows a little about everything — heart, lungs, skin, bones, and so on. When something is beyond their expertise, they refer you to a specialist.

A dermatologist, on the other hand, has spent years of extra training specifically focused on skin, hair, and nails. This means they can recognize rare and complex skin conditions that a general doctor might miss, and they have specialized tools and techniques for treating them.
The Bigger Picture — What Field Do They Belong To?

A dermatologist practices a medical field called dermatology. Dermatology is the branch of medicine dedicated entirely to the study, diagnosis, and treatment of skin, hair, and nail conditions. A dermatologist is simply the person who has qualified and is licensed to practice in that field.
When Would You See a Dermatologist?

You would visit a dermatologist when:

  • You have a persistent skin problem (like acne that won't go away, or a rash you can't explain)
  • You notice a suspicious mole or growth on your skin
  • You are losing hair abnormally
  • You have a nail problem that isn't getting better
  • Your general doctor refers you to one
  • You want a cosmetic skin treatment

A dermatologist is a fully trained medical doctor who has further specialized in everything to do with skin, hair, and nails — diagnosing diseases, performing procedures, and sometimes improving appearance.
